cells.tense: Right now the beginner's eyes are open and you are here with them.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Sit with a sprout in your care longer than usual before deciding anything about it. Give it only what it actually shows you it wants, in small amounts, no catch-up.
cells.core:
You can meet something unfamiliar without needing to name it first. A beginner's eyes look at what hasn't happened yet and don't rush to decide what it is. Where things are small and growing, you give them that room. Something new gets to stay new around you for a while. That is rare, and it is the whole of it.

Give the same attention to a sprout in your care. Feel which way it's already leaning, then feed that and nothing else. It will not match the plan you had. Motivation comes back out of genuine interest, not forcing — the fire stays warm when you're following something real rather than holding a shape. When you follow what's actually there, the care does the directing. You'll know by how much lighter the work feels the next morning.
cells.sheetLine: You meet new things with a beginner's eyes.
cells.verb: Approaching the unfamiliar with a beginner's wonder, feeling forward before understanding
cells.place: Where you tend what is small and not yet rooted

cells.tense: You are already living past this moment, braced for the result you can't write yet.
cells.act: tend the small thing and learn from it
cells.ask: Look after a sprout this season without trying to grow it on purpose. Do only what it asks, and let whatever happens next happen without steering it.
cells.core:
You're braced for what hasn't happened yet. Where you tend something, the version that could still fail is the one you can see — so you're already working on it, coaching it, holding it a stage ahead of where it is. It looks like care. From the other side it reads as a thing kept from becoming what it is. What you're tending is here, not the future of it.

You can't think your way out of pre-living. Tend a sprout without trying to make it anything. Water it, move it toward the light, do only what it asks. That's the whole job. What the plant does next is not the point — and some of what you're holding up will have to move at its own pace while you wait. The waiting is part of the work, not a delay before it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the future open instead of letting the thing grow.

cells.tense: You are still standing at the door of something that already opened behind you.
cells.act: follow a raw curiosity with no use for it
cells.ask: Chase a small curiosity about a sprout you look after, with nothing to do with what it turns up. Let whatever you find stay useless.
cells.core:
You used to meet new things with wide eyes. That door is behind you now, and what's left is doing what will work — planting what you've planted before, looking after what you can predict. The new thing doesn't come near the beds. Nothing in your care is being seen with fresh eyes right now. The room for surprise has gone quiet.

You can't push feeling into a tired place. Follow one curiosity with no use for it. Ask a question about a sprout whose answer you don't have, then watch for what it actually does. Let the answer stay useless. Understanding returns through following one real question, not through meaning to care more. A small raw curiosity, watched, shows you something new is still happening, even now.
cells.sheetLine: You care for what will surely grow.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room you are already writing.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Over the next month, keep a plain list of what you actually do for a sprout you look after. Actions only, no feeling words, no story.
cells.core:
You are already making the openings — trying a different spot, slowing down, saying the right thing at the right time — and if anyone asked, you'd call it luck or circumstance. It isn't. In the place you tend what's small, those choices are yours, and you file them under accident. The plants don't file it that way. They met the hand that chose.

Writing it down doesn't make it more yours. It lets you see what has been yours and not claimed. One page, plain: what you actually did, what changed, what you didn't have to do but did. Keep it to actions. The facts hold the practice steady, and practice that holds grows back into the hands that made it. What you find will likely be simpler than what you've been telling yourself. That is the point.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: I locate the over-care in a future that has not happened — a plant that is fine but not yet rooted, a result not yet shown — which the person may say is just ordinary worry, not a signature. The reader could also object that 'waiting for proof' describes anyone with a new thing. The ask survives being wrong because tending one sprout by doing only what it asks is still a thing to do on any Tuesday, regardless of why. The sentence that serves me more than them: any line about the seedling proving itself, which flatters the armchair diagnosis rather than handing them a move.
